title: Why You Can't Tickle Yourself
voiceover: Why can't you tickle yourself? In 1998, Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith studied exactly that. A robot touched people's palm, or they moved a robot arm to produce the touch themselves. People rated self-produced touch as less ticklish, less intense and less pleasant. When the researchers added a delay of up to 200 milliseconds between your movement and the touch, it felt progressively more ticklish. They proposed that your brain predicts the sensory results of your own movements. That prediction helps cancel the sensation when you cause it yourself. Brain scans showed less cerebellum activity for a movement that produced the touch than for one that didn't. So your brain treats touches you cause differently from touches caused by someone else. Tomorrow: why does everything take longer than you planned?

description: Why can't you tickle yourself? A 1998 experiment found self-produced touch felt less ticklish than the same touch from a robot, and the brain appears to predict the sensory result of your own movements. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Blakemore, S.-J., Wolpert, D. M., & Frith, C. D. (1998). Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation. Nature Neuroscience, 1(7), 635-640.
accuracy_note: Blakemore et al. (1998) used a robot-controlled touch task with small samples in a lab; 'the cerebellum is involved in predicting' is the authors' interpretation. The video describes tendencies from this study only.
